extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze what propositions mean and what is the immediate object of belief in a proposition (predication, classes, connotation vs. denotation), and classify the kinds of matters-of-fact propositions assert. Aimed at understanding the logical analysis of propositions and the grounds of truth and falsity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary object of belief in a proposition: facts/phenomena (not ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The immediate object of belief in a proposition is the thing or matter of fact signified by it — the external phenomena themselves — rather than merely the ideas or conceptions in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Believing is an act having for its subject the facts themselves, though a previous mental conception of the facts is an indispensable condition. Example: when we say 'fire causes heat' we mean the natural phenomenon fire causes the natural phenomenon heat, not that my idea of fire causes my idea of heat. Anti-pattern: treating belief as only manipulation of ideas (studying things 'at second hand') leads to a misleading theory of judgment and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of logic-as-relation-between-ideas error
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a fatal error to take the logician’s primary task as analyzing the relation between ideas (subject and predicate ideas) rather than relations between the corresponding phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This misconception caused stagnation in logic: treat propositions as concerning actual phenomena; recognizing this error explains why many discoveries in logical principles arose from natural science methods rather than from modern logicians' speculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes's theory of predication (names-of-same-thing account)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes: in every proposition what is signified is the speaker's belief that the predicate is a name of the same thing of which the subject is a name; if so, the proposition is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analysis is rigorously true only for propositions where both subject and predicate are proper names (e.g., 'Hyde was Clarendon'). It is a very limited account and fails for connotative/general names. Example counter-case: 'All men are mortal' — the meaning lies in attributes, not mere name identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation (attributes) vs denotation (individuals) — source of meaning for general names
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for proper names (and some abstract non-connotative names), the meaning of a name resides in its connotation — the set of attributes it conveys — rather than in the denotation (the particular individuals it names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing propositions with connotative terms, focus on the connotation (attributes) to understand what is asserted. Example: 'man' denotes the attributes constituting man; 'mortal' connotes the attribute of eventual death. The truth of 'All men are mortal' depends on the accompanying of one set of attributes by another, not on a prior naming convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: General names signify attributes grounded in phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: General names are names of indefinite sets of things possessing certain definite attributes; the attributes themselves are grounded in phenomena (external sense impressions or internal consciousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, propositions about general names assert co-existence or sequence of phenomena/attributes. Example: discovering that 'diamond is combustible' was empirical — found by sensory experiment — not derivable from word-meaning alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes are not pre-determined lists; classification follows attributes discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: It is erroneous to suppose general names/classes were formed by fixed, preordained lists of individuals; rather, classes are determined by attributes and may include unknown, future, or newly discovered instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the picture of framers of language having enumerated all class-members. The class-name's meaning is stable only as a name of all things (past, present, future) possessing certain attributes. This undercuts treating predication as mere reference to a pre-existing roll of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal affirmative propositions assert constant accompaniment of attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: A universal affirmative (e.g., 'All men are mortal') asserts that the attributes connoted by the predicate constantly accompany the attributes connoted by the subject: wherever the subject-attributes are found, the predicate-attributes will be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not about particular known individuals but about indefinite members sharing attributes. The proposition does not specify when (time) an attribute occurs, only that it does at some time (e.g., mortality at some time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions about substances/noumena are grounded in phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: When propositions assert facts about substances or attributes (noumena), their foundation is always assertions concerning the phenomena these entities exhibit; we can only meaningfully assert these via the observable phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., saying 'Socrates was contemporary with the Peloponnesian war' rests on observed series of facts (phenomena) attributed to Socrates and to the war. Predicating existence of a noumenon thus amounts to asserting causation or co-existence of phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five exhaustive kinds of matters-of-fact asserted by non-verbal propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every substantive (non-merely-verbal) proposition asserts one of five kinds of matter-of-fact: Existence, Co-existence, Sequence, Causation, or Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This five-fold division is presented as exhaustive of all things that can be believed or propounded as questions/answers. Use these categories to classify what a proposition asserts. (Examples and further distinctions follow in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance as distinct kind of assertion (especially for sensations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some propositions (notably those naming sensations) assert resemblance — that a present sensation is like previously experienced sensations — and this is a distinct kind of matter-of-fact not reducible usefully to sequence or co-existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While many class-predications involve resemblance implicitly, class-names grounded on unanalyzable resemblance (e.g., sensations like 'white') truly assert likeness. When names are applied by courtesy to borderline members (e.g., anomalous genera at a family's borders), the predicate may effectively affirm resemblance and nothing more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction in propositions of co-existence: Order in Place vs Co-inherence of Attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Professor Bain's distinction: one kind of co-existence accounts for 'Order in Place' (spatial arrangement), while another is 'Co-inherence of Attributes' — concurrence of attributes or powers in the same part/locality (e.g., properties of a mass of gold or mental faculties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is important: Order in Place deals with spatial arrangement, while co-inherence pertains to simultaneous attributes (sometimes potential) in the same entity. Co-inherence is still a case of co-existence of states of consciousness, often potential rather than actual (e.g., saying snow is white in darkness because the color will be perceived when light returns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: explaining classification by post hoc generalization (ὕστερον προτέρον)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a logical error to explain a judgment by invoking a conception that presupposes the judgment (explaining cause by effect). For example, treating classification as if people formed classes by first conceiving classes then assigning individuals presumes what it should explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing propositions, do not assume classes or the conception of classes pre-existed the judgments that led to them; classification often follows from successive judgments and observations rather than precedes them.

rubrics_metrics.name: When predicate is general name, proposition sometimes merely affirms resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases where a general name is predicated, the assertion is not that the object possesses the full properties of the class but that it either possesses them or at least resembles the class more than any other; in such cases the predicate affirms resemblance rather than full connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This occurs especially for borderline members admitted by courtesy into a class (e.g., substances called metals with few metal-typical properties). Scientific formulations may qualify such predications with wording like 'is considered' or 'may be ranked as'.
